lines.text: A land of forests and marshes between Poland and Russia, fought over for centuries. This is the story of Belarus, from old Polotsk to today.
The story begins in Polotsk, first written of in 862, one of the oldest cities of the East Slavs.
Two centuries later Minsk appears in the records, the town that would grow into the capital.
From the thirteenth century these lands became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, a great state stretching across Eastern Europe.
In Polotsk, Francysk Skaryna was born, who would print the first Bible in the Belarusian language.
In the sixteenth century the red-brick Mir Castle rose in the west of the country.
In 1569 Lithuania joined Poland in a Commonwealth with an elected king, for a time among the largest states in Europe.
At Nesvizh, the powerful Radziwill family built their palace and castle.
In 1746 Tadeusz Kosciuszko was born here, who fought for freedom in America and in Poland.
By then Russia had taken these lands, and in 1836 work began on the great fortress at Brest.
In 1882 Yanka Kupala was born, the poet who would give Belarusians a national voice.
Five years later, in Vitebsk, came Marc Chagall, who painted the town's rooftops and floating lovers for the rest of his life.
On the Polish border lies Bialowieza Forest, one of Europe's last primeval woods and home of the European bison.
In 1941 the German army invaded. In three years of occupation, about a quarter of the people of Belarus died.
In 1943 the village of Khatyn was burned with its people inside, one of hundreds of villages destroyed.
In the summer of 1944 the Soviet offensive called Bagration swept the Germans out of Belarus.
In 1948 Svetlana Alexievich was born, the writer who recorded ordinary people's voices and won the Nobel Prize in 2015.
In 1954 came Alexander Lukashenko, who would rule the country from 1994.
And in 1982, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, who would one day lead the opposition from exile.
In 1986 the reactor at Chernobyl exploded just south of the border, and radioactive fallout came down across Belarus.
In 1991, as the Soviet Union ended, Belarus became an independent country, with Minsk as its capital.
It was in a Belarusian forest that year that leaders signed the Belovezha Accords, which ended the Soviet Union.
In 2020, after an election many saw as stolen, huge crowds filled the streets, and the protests were crushed.
Through war and changing borders, Belarus has kept its own name and its own voice.
